The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! What makes a good café? The criteria depend on the coffee drinker. Maybe you’re a purist who’s obsessed with direct sourcing of single-origin beans. Maybe you’re a nerd, in which case you’re all about the latest laboratory-like brewing method. Or maybe you prefer a place that serves up sweet and seasonal drinks, with comfy couches upon which to plop and enjoy them. The latest batch of cafés to open around Chittenden County isn’t fussy. None of them has a pour-over on the menu or a siphon behind the bar. But they all make a good cup of coffee — or tea, if that’s your thing. And alongside the lattes and local pastries, they serve a big dose of charm, from interactive art to stacks of books. We headed to five spots that opened this year to sip seasonal lattes, dirty sodas, classic espresso drinks and cold-foam chai. Since the founding of the city, Parisians had been burying their dead in the middle of town, which led to an untenable situation: In the spring of 1780, heavy rains wrecked a burial mound at the overcrowded Les Innocents cemetery, sending a wave of decaying corpses tumbling into the building next door. The king’s solution to necrotic overpopulation? Shut down all of Paris’s graveyards and transfer all the bodies to an extensive network of underground tunnels left behind by 13th-century limestone miners—a task that took 12 years to complete. Today, morbid-minded tourists—like our @cntraveler editorial operations manager, @tayloreisenhauer, who captured these photos—can visit @catacombesdeparis_officiel. There, you can explore about a mile of this underground labyrinth’s 200 miles of bone-lined walls, greeted by this friendly inscription: "Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la mort" (Stop! This is the empire of death).

Someone tell Belle I found her library in Vermont. 📚♥️ The @stjohnsburyathenaeum is straight out of Beauty and the Beast, with ornate woodwork and spiral staircases inside a building that’s been welcoming readers for more than 150 years. It’s such an unusual find in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, right on Main Street, and the library is only part of the reason to visit. Horace Fairbanks gave the Athenaeum to the community in 1871, and it opened with 8,000 books. I love that it still serves as the town’s public library. Imagine getting to call this your neighborhood reading spot, with sunlight coming through those tall, arched windows while you settle into a book. Then there’s the art gallery, added in 1873, where paintings in heavy gilded frames hang one above another in a setting that preserves the feel of a 19th-century museum. New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. Then on Sunday, August 4th, 1929, nearly ten thousand people packed City Hall Park to watch Burlington's last street car burn. Now, 100 years later, @ridegmt faces a $3 million shortfall that threatens 30% of its service. Same as the street cars, our public transit faces an existential lack of public investment. These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

Sonar with a side of squeaks! Bats have a remarkable ability called echolocation, which allows them to navigate in the dark by making high-pitched sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. Essentially, they shout into the void and wait for the void to explain where everything is. Same. Still waiting… These sound waves help bats locate insects, avoid obstacles, and navigate their surroundings with impressive accuracy. They can even detect objects as small as human hair. Meanwhile, some humans have been known to walk into a glass door in broad daylight. One time. Moving on. Bats are an important part of many national park ecosystems, helping control insect populations and keeping nature ticking along after dark. So, the next time you hear a bat making noises, remember it isn’t screaming into the darkness. Well, it is, but it’s using a highly sophisticated biological sonar system. Screaming with purpose. Try it. Watch out for that door. NPS Photos: Bats flying in the darkness

Oh, so THAT’S what an “ongoing” work means…. Swing by “Catalyst: Art as Inquiry” before it closes on December 12, 2026. And even if you’d seen, Heimo Wallner’s “Last Note (Echo),” 2026 before, you’re going to want to take another look. From the artist: I draw, and this ongoing process manifests itself in piles of drawings, animations and when possible: room drawings—made quickly, with a clear deadline, these wall drawings force me to generate imagery on the spot and little strands of narratives crystallize, interweave, connect, and disrupt. They become rhythm, texture, ornament: wallpaper. The human condition is my quarry. Stupidity (my own and the general)—an endless source. The banal and the essential, daily news vs eternal truths, private painful secrets turn into practical jokes—catharsis and damnation all at once.

We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Formerly Sugarsnap Farm, Wet Foot Farm is now owned and operated by Patrick Shafer, Jamie Cohen, and Abbey Duke. They’re one of seven farm operations growing food on land leased from the Intervale Center! Alongside produce for Sugarsnap Catering, the farm grows pawpaws—North America’s largest native edible fruit. With a creamy texture and hints of mango and banana, pawpaws naturally grow in moist forests and along waterways. Adapted to periodic flooding, these perennial trees support healthy ecosystems by stabilizing soil, reducing erosion, and providing wildlife habitat. Their resilience makes them a promising crop for climate-resilient agriculture. Pawpaw trees take several years to produce fruit, making growing them a long-term investment. Abbey Duke planted the original pawpaw trees in 2010 and in 2021, Patrick and Jamie began cultivating and planting more trees to meet growing demand, and they plan to continue expanding production in the coming years. Our Intervale Conservation Nursery grows thousands of native trees and shrubs each year, but our work doesn’t stop there! 🌱 This year, our Nursery Crew is also caring for 50 acres of young forests across Vermont. At Riverside Park in Warren, we’re working with the Town of Waitsfield and Friends of the Mad River to restore 2 acres along the Mad River. Along with removing invasive knotweed around young trees, we’re building living barriers from willow branches that take root and sprout! These natural barriers will help stabilize riverbanks, prevent invasive knotweed from spreading, and protect water quality throughout the Lake Champlain Basin. Healthy rivers and soils are the foundation of healthy farms and food systems! This critical stewardship work to restore riparian forest buffers is possible thanks to funding from the Lake Champlain Basin Program and Great Lakes Fishery Commission. THE hottest color of the season is hunter orange! Not only does fluorescent orange make a chic fashion statement, but more importantly, it keeps hunters and all outdoor recreators visible to other people in the woods. Wearing a hunter orange hat or vest is important for everyone in the woods during hunting season. Whether you're hunting, bird watching, or trail running, bright orange can help you be seen, even in low-light. While it isn’t recommended to wear orange during waterfowl and turkey seasons, we do still suggest folks chasing fall ducks, geese and turkey wear hunter orange when going to and from blind tree stands or calling spots. Same goes for bowhunters walking up to their treestands or climbing down at the end of the day. Be smart and safe outdoors this fall. Wear orange!

The sandy seafloor that looks empty to us but is teeming with life. And of course the coral reefs that support a quarter of all marine species. These ocean habitats face many pressures, and how seafood is caught and farmed is one of them. We might actually call that a success. The minute a restaurant opens, its days are numbered. Could be 2 years, it could be 20 years. It’s what a restaurant accomplishes in that time that makes the difference and we’re proud of what we did here. 🪬 Come by today for the last hurrah. Our friends at @highergroundmusic are welcoming vocalist and violin virtuoso L. Shankar to the Showcase Lounge on Monday, October 12! Known for introducing South Indian music to Western audiences, Shankar has built a remarkable career with his innovative 10-string stereophonic Double Violin and collaborations with artists including Peter Gabriel, Phil Collins, Madonna, Frank Zappa, and many more. He'll be joined by SelvaGanesh Vinayakram on kanjira (frame drum), Amit Kavthekar on tabla (hand percussion), and Swaminathan SelvaGanesh on ghatam (Udu pot or clay pot). We know our Lane Series audience appreciates extraordinary musicianship, and this is a performance we think you'll love! Doors open at 7:00 PM! Learn more and get tickets: highergroundmusic.com
